WORRY GUIDE — LIFE

When you're torn over a relationship

A friend who leaves you tired after you meet, someone at work you can't say what you want to say to, family who feel so close it is stifling. Being torn over a relationship happens between caring about the other person and wanting to protect yourself. It is not only a choice between cutting ties and carrying on; adjusting the distance is an option too. This page offers perspectives for sorting out the decision you're torn over in how you relate to people, and introduces the tarot cards connected to it.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

Anxiety about how the other person will see you is deeply involved in being torn over a relationship. As you wonder whether putting distance between you would make them dislike you, or whether saying no would break the relationship, you end up putting your own feelings last. A long history together, or feeling indebted to someone, also makes judgment harder. You may also be assuming that if you just put up with it, everything will settle. Start by looking back at how you feel after spending time with that person. Whether you feel at ease or tired is an important clue.

POINT 02

How to sort it out

The key to sorting this out is to think not in terms of whether to continue or cut off the relationship, but in terms of what distance feels comfortable. There are several ways to reduce the burden while keeping the relationship: meeting less often, choosing your topics, or meeting in a group rather than one-to-one. Writing out what you want from the other person and what they want from you can also reveal where the mismatch lies. Check, too, whether you are tying yourself up with assumptions. Much of what feels like the relationship would end if you said no turns out, when you actually try it, to be surprisingly fine.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn over a relationship, cards that speak to being bound by assumptions, anxiety, connection, and attachment can offer useful clues.

The Eight of Swords shows someone blindfolded and surrounded by swords who can, in fact, walk away on their own, reflecting a mind that has become unable to move because of its own assumptions.

The Nine of Swords shows someone unable to sleep at night, worrying, pointing to a state where anxiety is swelling inside your head.

The Two of Cups points to an equal relationship of mutual respect, while

The Devil represents an attachment where you want to leave but cannot. From the card you drew, consider whether what is binding you is the other person or your own assumptions.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions. After meeting that person, how do you feel? Are you continuing the relationship because you like them, out of a sense of obligation, or because you are afraid of being disliked? If you shared how you truly feel, would the relationship really break? If you changed the distance a little, what could you do? If you were in the other person's position, would you want them to tell you honestly? None of these questions has a single right answer. What matters is simply not continuing to ignore your own feelings — that is the foundation for building a calm relationship that lasts.

CARDS

Cards connected to this decision

  • Eight of Swords

    A card that reflects a mind unable to move because of its own assumptions.

  • Nine of Swords

    A state where anxiety swells in your head, worrying so much you cannot sleep.

  • Two of Cups

    Shows what an equal relationship of mutual respect looks like.

  • The Devil

    Helps you notice dependence or attachment — wanting to leave but being unable to.

  • The Hermit

    The importance of taking time alone to look again at your own feelings.

Change how you relate, or put some distance between you? Why not think about a choice you can live with without straining yourself?
